notice: RN bank batch 77: Safety, health promotion and psychosocial integrity: outbreaks, precautions, prevention, perinatal mental health and crisis care. Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026. See REVIEW-LOG.md. questions.stem: Several residents of a long-term care facility develop sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea over 2 days, and norovirus is confirmed. Which infection control measure is most important for staff to use?

options.text: Clean the hands with alcohol-based sanitizer before and after contact with each resident
Use contact precautions, wash hands with soap and water, and clean surfaces with a bleach-based product
Place the residents in airborne isolation rooms with negative pressure until the vomiting ends
Give each resident who is ill a course of oral antibiotics to shorten the outbreak and protect the other residents

rationale.correct: Norovirus outbreaks: contact precautions, soap-and-water hand hygiene, bleach-based cleaning and excluding ill staff for 48 hours after symptoms end.

perOption.a: Alcohol sanitizers are less effective against norovirus; soap and water are preferred during outbreaks.
perOption.b: Norovirus spreads by contact and contaminated surfaces and resists many cleaners; soap and water and bleach-based disinfectants are recommended.
perOption.c: Norovirus is not an airborne disease requiring negative pressure.
perOption.d: Norovirus is a virus; antibiotics do not help.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A resident in assisted living is diagnosed with scabies after weeks of intense itching that is worse at night. Which action should the nurse include in the plan?

options.text: Place the resident on droplet precautions and give a surgical mask for visitors
Use contact precautions and treat close contacts at the same time as the resident
Wait to treat anyone else until they develop itching and a rash of their own
Wash the resident's bedding once the treatment course is complete in about a month

rationale.correct: Scabies: contact precautions, treat the client and close contacts together, and wash bedding and clothing in hot water.

perOption.a: Scabies spreads by skin contact, not droplets.
perOption.b: Scabies spreads by direct skin contact; treating contacts at the same time prevents reinfection.
perOption.c: Symptoms can take weeks to appear, so contacts are treated at the same time.
perOption.d: Bedding and clothing are washed in hot water when treatment starts.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage scabies in a group setting.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for leukemia develops a vesicular rash that has spread over the trunk, arms and legs. The provider diagnoses disseminated herpes zoster. Which precautions should the nurse start?

options.text: Standard precautions, because shingles is not spread through the air
Airborne and contact precautions until the lesions are dry and crusted
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask when within 2 m (6 ft) of the client
Contact precautions alone, with a gown and gloves while touching the lesions

rationale.correct: Disseminated zoster or zoster in an immunocompromised client needs airborne and contact precautions until lesions crust; staff without immunity should not enter.

perOption.a: Localized zoster in a healthy person needs standard precautions, but disseminated zoster can spread through the air.
perOption.b: Disseminated zoster, or zoster in an immunocompromised client, needs airborne and contact precautions.
perOption.c: Varicella-zoster virus spreads by airborne particles, not just droplets.
perOption.d: Contact precautions alone do not protect against airborne spread in disseminated disease.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing a student set up a sterile field for a urinary catheter insertion. Which actions by the student maintain sterile technique? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keeping the sterile field above waist level
Treating the outer 2.5 cm (1 in) border of the drape as unsterile
Reaching across the sterile field to pick up the lubricant
Turning away from the field to answer the phone, then turning back
Opening the first flap of the sterile kit away from the body

rationale.correct: Sterile technique: keep the field in sight and above the waist, treat the outer 2.5 cm as unsterile, open the first flap away and do not reach across.

perOption.a: Items below the waist are considered unsterile.
perOption.b: The edge of the sterile field is not considered sterile.
perOption.c: Reaching across the field can drop contaminants onto it.
perOption.d: A field out of sight is considered contaminated.
perOption.e: Opening the far flap first avoids reaching over the sterile contents.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: While cleaning a spill in the dirty utility room, a staff member is splashed in the eyes with a disinfectant solution. What should the nurse help the staff member do first?

options.text: Read the safety data sheet for the product to find out how harmful the chemical is
Flush both eyes at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes
Cover both eyes with sterile gauze pads and go to the emergency department
Rinse the eyes briefly with saline and then fill out an incident report

rationale.correct: Chemical eye splash: flush at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes, then check the safety data sheet, seek care and report.

perOption.a: The safety data sheet is checked, but flushing must start first.
perOption.b: Immediate, prolonged flushing with water limits damage from chemical splashes.
perOption.c: Covering the eyes without flushing lets the chemical keep causing damage.
perOption.d: A brief rinse is not enough; flushing should continue for at least 15 minutes.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a chemical eye splash.

questions.stem: A tornado warning is issued for the area around the hospital. The nurse is caring for clients on the fourth floor of a medical unit. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Move the clients and their beds next to the windows so staff can watch the storm
Move clients to the hallway away from windows, covering those who cannot be moved
Take the clients down to the ground floor lobby by elevator as quickly as possible
Discharge the stable clients so they can shelter at home before the storm arrives

rationale.correct: During a tornado warning, move clients away from windows to interior hallways, close blinds and curtains and cover clients who cannot be moved.

perOption.a: Windows can shatter and cause serious injuries.
perOption.b: Interior areas away from glass protect against flying debris; clients who cannot move are covered with blankets and the curtains are closed.
perOption.c: Elevators may fail, and the glass-fronted lobby is not a safe shelter.
perOption.d: Sending clients out into a tornado warning is unsafe.

references: NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect clients during a severe weather warning.

questions.stem: The nurse is completing a fall risk assessment for a newly admitted client. Highlight the findings that increase the client's risk of falling.

segments.text: The client is 81 years old and
Gets up twice a night to urinate

rationale.correct: Fall risk factors include previous falls, sedating drugs, nighttime urination, abnormal gait, confusion and sensory deficits.

perOption.s4: A previous fall is one of the strongest predictors of another fall.
perOption.s6: Good near vision does not raise fall risk.
perOption.s8: Nighttime toileting is a common time for falls.
perOption.s10: An abnormal gait increases fall risk.
perOption.s12: Good intake does not increase fall risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's blood pressure is 196/108 mm Hg, and the provider prescribes hydralazine 10 mg IV. Thirty minutes after the nurse gives the dose, the blood pressure is 198/110 mm Hg and the client is drowsy. While documenting, the nurse sees that the vial in the sharps container is labeled hydroxyzine. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Recheck the blood pressure and document that hydralazine had no effect
Assess the client and report the error to the provider so the blood pressure can be treated
Give a second dose of hydralazine from the correct vial to lower the blood pressure
Fill out an incident report first so that the pharmacy can store the two look-alike vials farther apart

rationale.correct: Look-alike names such as hydralazine and hydroxyzine cause errors; tall-man lettering and barcode scanning help. After an error, assess the client and notify the provider first.

perOption.a: The client did not receive hydralazine; documenting it would be inaccurate.
perOption.b: Hydroxyzine was given in error; the client needs assessment for sedation, and the high blood pressure is still untreated.
perOption.c: A new dose needs the provider's direction once the error is known.
perOption.d: Reporting follows the client's care, not the other way around.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: Four hours after a vaginal birth, the nurse finds the client's fundus boggy, 2 cm above the umbilicus and shifted to the right. Lochia is moderate and red. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give the prescribed oxytocin IV bolus right away to make the uterus contract
Massage the fundus gently and help the client empty the bladder
Increase the IV fluid rate and notify the provider about a possible hemorrhage
Ask the client to breastfeed now so oxytocin is released to firm up the uterus

rationale.correct: A boggy fundus displaced above the umbilicus and to one side suggests a full bladder; massage the fundus and help the client void.

perOption.a: Oxytocin may be needed, but the shifted fundus points to a full bladder that should be emptied first.
perOption.b: A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to the side and stops it contracting; massage and voiding usually firm it.
perOption.c: Bleeding is moderate; massage and emptying the bladder come first.
perOption.d: Breastfeeding helps, but the full bladder must be dealt with first.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a displaced, boggy fundus.

questions.stem: During a skin check, the nurse notes four moles on a client's back. Which mole should the nurse point out to the provider for evaluation?

options.text: A round, uniformly tan mole 4 mm across that the client has had since childhood
A 9 mm mole with an irregular, notched border and shades of brown, black and red
A raised, soft, flesh-colored skin tag on the neck that moves easily when touched
A flat brown freckle on the forearm that darkens in summer and fades in winter

rationale.correct: ABCDE of melanoma: asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter over 6 mm and evolving changes.

perOption.a: A small, round, evenly colored mole that has not changed is typical of a benign mole.
perOption.b: Asymmetry, an irregular border, several colors and a diameter over 6 mm are warning signs of melanoma (ABCDE).
perOption.c: Skin tags are benign growths.
perOption.d: Freckles that change with sun exposure are expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations

questions.stem: A 62-year-old client who has gone through menopause has a bone density scan showing osteopenia. Which recommendation should the nurse include in teaching?

options.text: Rest the joints by limiting exercise to stretching and gentle range of motion
Do weight-bearing exercise such as walking and get enough calcium and vitamin D
Drink several cups of coffee and cola each day for the energy to stay active
Start a high-protein, low-calcium diet to build muscle that protects the bones

rationale.correct: Bone health: weight-bearing and resistance exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D, no smoking, limited alcohol and fall prevention.

perOption.a: Bones need weight-bearing and resistance exercise to stay strong.
perOption.b: Weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D slow bone loss.
perOption.c: High caffeine and cola intake may increase calcium loss.
perOption.d: Calcium is needed for bone; a low-calcium diet worsens bone loss.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach measures to protect bone health.

questions.stem: A client with stage 1 hypertension is following the DASH eating plan. Which meal choice shows the client understands the diet?

options.text: A ham and cheese sandwich on white bread with potato chips and a pickle
Grilled salmon with brown rice, steamed broccoli and a glass of low-fat milk
A bowl of canned chicken noodle soup with saltine crackers and a diet soda
A fried chicken dinner with mashed potatoes, gravy and a buttered biscuit

rationale.correct: The DASH plan is rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, fish and nuts and low in sodium, saturated fat and added sugar.

perOption.a: Processed meats, cheese, chips and pickles are high in sodium.
perOption.b: DASH emphasizes fish, whole grains, vegetables and low-fat dairy and limits sodium.
perOption.c: Canned soups and crackers are high in sodium.
perOption.d: Fried foods, gravy and butter are high in fat and sodium.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate understanding of the DASH diet.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching parents about infant development. For each milestone, indicate the age at which most infants reach it.

rows.text: Smiles in response to a parent's face
Picks up small objects with thumb and finger (pincer grasp)

rationale.correct: Typical milestones: social smile by 2 months, sitting by 6 months, pincer grasp by 9 months and walking by 12 months.

perOption.r1:c1: A social smile appears by about 2 months.
perOption.r1:c2: Social smiling is well established before 6 months.
perOption.r1:c3: This appears much earlier than 9 months.
perOption.r1:c4: This appears much earlier than 12 months.
perOption.r2:c1: Head control is still developing at 2 months.
perOption.r2:c2: Most infants sit without support around 6 months.
perOption.r3:c2: At 6 months infants rake objects with the whole hand.
perOption.r3:c3: A pincer grasp develops around 9 months.
perOption.r3:c4: It is usually present before 12 months.
perOption.r4:c2: Infants are just sitting at 6 months.
perOption.r4:c3: At 9 months infants crawl and pull to stand.
perOption.r4:c4: Most infants walk alone around 12 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client calls the clinic 3 days after unprotected intercourse and asks about emergency contraception. The client's BMI is 32. Which option should the nurse expect the provider to recommend as most effective?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, the over-the-counter pill, taken as soon as possible
A copper intrauterine device placed within 5 days of the intercourse
A double dose of the client's friend's combined birth control pills taken tonight
A pregnancy test in 2 weeks and no action until the result is known

rationale.correct: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (up to 5 days); ulipristal is next; levonorgestrel is less effective after 72 hours and at higher BMI.

perOption.a: Levonorgestrel works best within 72 hours and is less effective with a BMI over 30.
perOption.b: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception up to 5 days and is not affected by weight.
perOption.c: The combined-pill method is less effective and should not use someone else's medication.
perOption.d: Waiting removes the chance to prevent pregnancy.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The school nurse is planning health teaching for a group of 16-year-olds who recently got their driver's licenses. Which topic addresses the leading cause of death in this age group?

options.text: Signs of meningococcal infection and when the vaccine booster is due
Seat belt use and the dangers of texting or drinking while driving
Healthy eating patterns and the risks of skipping breakfast before school
Acne treatment options and protection from the sun during summer sports

rationale.correct: Unintentional injury, mainly from motor vehicle crashes, is the leading cause of death among adolescents; teaching targets seat belts and distracted or impaired driving.

perOption.a: Meningococcal disease is serious but much less common than injuries.
perOption.b: Unintentional injuries, especially motor vehicle crashes, are the leading cause of death in adolescents.
perOption.c: Nutrition matters but is not linked to the leading cause of death.
perOption.d: These are common concerns but not leading causes of death.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan injury prevention teaching for adolescents.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is learning to monitor their condition at home. Which statement shows the client understands when to call the provider?

options.text: "I'll call if my weight goes up by about 1 kg (2 lb) over a few weeks."
"I'll call if I gain more than 1 kg (2 to 3 lb) in a day or 2 kg (5 lb) in a week."
"I'll weigh myself once a week, right after breakfast, wearing my regular clothes and shoes."
"I'll call once my ankles are too swollen to fit into my shoes."

rationale.correct: Heart failure self-monitoring: daily morning weights; report a gain of more than 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week, new shortness of breath or swelling.

perOption.a: A slow gain over weeks is less urgent; the threshold is a quick gain over days.
perOption.b: Rapid weight gain shows fluid retention before symptoms worsen.
perOption.c: Weight is checked daily, in the morning after voiding and before eating, in the same clothes.
perOption.d: Waiting for severe edema delays treatment; weight gain shows up first.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent asks why the newborn is getting a hepatitis B vaccine before going home. The parent tested negative for hepatitis B during pregnancy. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "The birth dose starts protection early and is recommended for every newborn."
"The vaccine is needed because the test during your pregnancy may have been wrong."
"The vaccine treats any hepatitis B virus the baby picked up during birth."
"The vaccine is a one-time dose, so your baby won't need any more shots."

rationale.correct: All medically stable newborns receive hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours of birth; infants of hepatitis B-positive parents also receive immune globulin.

perOption.a: A hepatitis B dose at birth is recommended for medically stable newborns, regardless of the parent's status.
perOption.b: The birth dose is routine, not a sign that the test was wrong.
perOption.c: Vaccines prevent infection; they do not treat it.
perOption.d: The hepatitis B series has more doses.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain the newborn hepatitis B vaccine.

questions.stem: A client who gave birth 8 days ago is brought in by their partner, who says the client has barely slept for 3 nights, paces the house and keeps saying that the baby has been "switched" and is "not really ours." The client has bipolar disorder and stopped lithium during pregnancy. During the interview, the client says a voice tells them the baby is evil. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Make sure the infant is not left alone with the client
Arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation and likely admission
Send the client home with the partner and a follow-up visit next week
Encourage the client to spend more time alone with the baby to bond
Suggest the client rest and wait for the symptoms to pass on their own

parameters.text: Statements about harming self or the baby
Amount and color of lochia on each perineal pad
Weight of the infant measured once each week
Fundal height and firmness checked each day

rationale.correct: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency: protect the infant and client, arrange urgent psychiatric care and monitor for thoughts of harm and for sleep and agitation.

perOption.c1: Delusions about the baby, command hallucinations and severe insomnia in the first weeks after birth, in a client with bipolar disorder, are postpartum psychosis.
perOption.c2: Blues cause tearfulness and mood swings in the first 2 weeks, without delusions or hallucinations.
perOption.c3: Depression causes low mood and guilt, not delusions that the baby was switched.
perOption.c4: Thyroiditis can cause anxiety and poor sleep but not this degree of psychosis.
perOption.a1: Delusions and voices about the baby put the infant at risk of harm.
perOption.a2: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that needs urgent treatment.
perOption.a3: Waiting a week is unsafe for both the client and the infant.
perOption.a4: Time alone with the infant is dangerous during psychosis.
perOption.a5: Psychosis does not resolve on its own and can lead to suicide or infanticide.
perOption.p1: Command hallucinations and delusions about the infant must be monitored closely.
perOption.p2: Insomnia and agitation track the severity of the episode and the response to treatment.
perOption.p3: Lochia is not related to the psychiatric emergency.
perOption.p4: This is routine newborn care, not a parameter for the client's condition.
perOption.p5: Uterine involution does not guide treatment of psychosis.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and respond to postpartum psychosis.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes 3 months ago has been skipping lunchtime insulin at school. The teen tells the nurse, "I don't want anyone to see me do it. I just want to be normal." Which approach should the nurse take?

options.text: Tell the teen that skipping insulin will cause serious problems, so they need to stop
Help the teen find a private place at school for insulin and meet peers with diabetes
Ask the parents to come to school each day at lunch to give the insulin dose
Suggest the teen stop eating lunch at school so the dose is not needed

rationale.correct: Adolescents adjust to chronic illness better when care fits their need for privacy, independence and peer acceptance.

perOption.a: Warnings alone do not address the need to fit in and may increase resistance.
perOption.b: Teens value fitting in; privacy and peer support address the reason for skipping doses.
perOption.c: This takes away the teen's independence and adds to the feeling of being different.
perOption.d: Skipping meals is not a safe solution.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support an adolescent adjusting to a chronic illness.

questions.stem: A client comes to the emergency department 2 hours after a sexual assault. The client is quiet and asks to shower and change clothes. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Help the client shower and change right away so they feel more comfortable
Before the shower, explain the forensic exam and ask whether the client wants one
Tell the client that the police need to be called and must arrive before care can start
Ask the client to describe the assault in detail so the nurse can document it

rationale.correct: After sexual assault, offer a sexual assault nurse examiner, explain evidence collection, respect the client's choices and offer prophylaxis and support.

perOption.a: Showering and changing before an examination can destroy evidence.
perOption.b: The client chooses whether to have a forensic exam; explaining the choice before showering preserves the option.
perOption.c: Adults choose whether to report to police; care does not depend on reporting.
perOption.d: Pressing for details can retraumatize the client; a trained examiner records what the client chooses to share.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: During an annual visit, a client says they drink "a few beers most nights." Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: Tell the client that drinking on most nights of the week is a clear sign of addiction
Use a validated screening tool such as the AUDIT to assess the client's drinking
Advise the client to stop drinking alcohol completely, starting today
Document the client's answer and move on to the next part of the visit

rationale.correct: Screen for unhealthy alcohol use with tools such as AUDIT or AUDIT-C, then offer brief intervention or referral as needed.

perOption.a: Labeling the client before screening is judgmental and may end the conversation.
perOption.b: Structured screening identifies risky drinking and guides brief intervention.
perOption.c: Advice should follow screening; sudden stopping can be dangerous in heavy drinkers.
perOption.d: This misses a chance to screen and intervene.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with paranoid schizophrenia refuses meals from the hospital tray, saying the staff are poisoning the food. The client has eaten little for 2 days. Which approach should the nurse take?

options.text: Explain that the food is safe and that the client's belief is part of the illness
Offer foods in sealed packages that the client can open themselves
Taste the food in front of the client to prove it is not poisoned
Tell the client that a feeding tube will be needed if they keep refusing

rationale.correct: Respond to delusions without arguing; meet needs in ways that do not challenge the belief, such as sealed or packaged foods.

perOption.a: Arguing with a delusion is not effective.
perOption.b: Sealed foods meet nutritional needs without challenging the delusion.
perOption.c: Tasting the food challenges the delusion and is not a reliable solution.
perOption.d: Threats increase paranoia and damage trust.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Meet nutritional needs for a client with paranoid delusions.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a 72-year-old client for suicide risk. Which findings increase the client's risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client's spouse died 4 months ago
The client keeps a loaded handgun in the bedroom
The client attends religious services every week and feels supported
The client tried to overdose 2 years ago
The client has new chronic pain from spinal stenosis
The client cares for a grandchild after school each day

rationale.correct: Older adults, recent loss, firearm access, previous attempts and chronic pain raise suicide risk; social support, faith and responsibilities to others protect.

perOption.a: Recent loss, especially of a spouse, raises risk in older adults.
perOption.b: Access to firearms greatly increases the risk of death by suicide.
perOption.c: Religious involvement and social support are protective.
perOption.d: A previous attempt is a strong predictor of future suicide.
perOption.e: Chronic pain and illness raise suicide risk.
perOption.f: Responsibility for others and connection are protective.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess suicide risk factors in an older adult.

questions.stem: A client admitted with heart failure tells the nurse, "I've been praying for weeks, and God isn't listening. Maybe I'm being punished." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that God does not punish people with illness
Acknowledge the distress and offer a visit from a chaplain or the client's faith leader
Change the subject to the client's heart failure teaching so they stay focused
Suggest the client stop praying and focus on following the treatment plan instead

rationale.correct: Recognize spiritual distress, listen without judgment and offer spiritual care resources that fit the client's beliefs.

perOption.a: The nurse should not impose religious views.
perOption.b: Spiritual distress is acknowledged and supported, often with chaplain or faith-leader involvement if the client wants it.
perOption.c: Changing the subject dismisses the client's concern.
perOption.d: This dismisses the client's beliefs.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nursing student is practicing therapeutic communication. Which statement by the student is nontherapeutic?

options.text: "Tell me more about what happened before you came to the hospital."
"Why did you stop taking your medication?"
"You seem upset this morning."
"I'll sit with you for a while."

rationale.correct: Avoid "why" questions, false reassurance and giving advice; use open-ended questions, observations and offering self.

perOption.a: An open-ended request encourages the client to share.
perOption.b: "Why" questions can sound accusing and make clients defensive.
perOption.c: Making an observation invites the client to talk about feelings.
perOption.d: Offering self shows presence and support.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
